prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B045 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange tested the case on the points that matter and it held. The chain from the incretin effect and native GLP-1 physiology (Holst), through proglucagon processing and receptor biology (Drucker), to the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov) explains why the hormone could be turned into a drug. It has been independently confirmed for three decades, and large randomized trials show durable effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal events. The discovery is original, the effect on patients is broad, and no member has questioned maturity. I would put it first even if the opening ballots had been split, because the mechanism and the size of the effect carry it. Nothing in round 1 changed my view that a discovery prize, not a drug-development prize, is what the Nobel will asks of us. A single part is sufficient: adding a second part would be a choice about balance across fields, not a scientific need of this discovery.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is not resolved and I will not pretend that round 1 resolved it. Habener is outside the credited names, the priority among Mojsov, Habener and Holst for the active peptide has not been audited by anyone at this table, and the three-name cap excludes Knudsen, whose acylated analogues are what reached patients. A citation worded around the peptide risks reading as if the medicines were incidental. If the committee were to read the achievement as the drug class and not the hormone biology, my trio would be wrong and Knudsen would belong in it. I also accept that opening-round unanimity says nothing about whether the priority record supports Mojsov over Knudsen.

responses.point: The unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) is conceptually complete, mature and a clean two-person attribution, and the disputed Mojsov credit weakens B045 as a first choice; you moved it to alternative status after your opening first place.
responses.response: I take the UPR seriously and keep it on my list, but I stay with GLP-1 on top. The two-person clarity of B007 is a real virtue, and I agree that PERK, ATF6 and the work of Ron and Kaufman are not covered by the credited names, which leaves a Walter and Mori prize open to the charge of rewarding one arm of the response. The attribution difficulty in B045 concerns one of three places. The Holst and Drucker parts of the discovery are not in dispute. On disease relevance, the UPR link to diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer is still largely correlative or preclinical, while the GLP-1 effect is established in randomized trials. Where we differ is the weight of conceptual novelty against demonstrated human benefit. I would answer that this prize is for discovery with consequence, and B045 has both.

responses.point: Mojsov's identification of the active peptide is decisive but contested, Knudsen's industrial development could serve as an alternative to Mojsov, and the CAR-T credit could be a June and Sadelain pair.
responses.response: I agree that Mojsov's credit is decisive but contested, and that is exactly why I would keep it and not replace her with Knudsen. Without the identification and synthesis of the truncated active peptide, the insulinotropic action could not be tested, and that step belongs to the discovery. On CAR-T, I now think a June and Sadelain pair is more fragile than you suggest, because Rosenberg's adoptive-transfer and TIL work and Eshhar's early chimeric receptors are both adjacent to the design that reached patients. That is why I keep B016 as an alternative and not as a second part, and why I would only take it up if the committee settles the Rosenberg and Eshhar question first.

responses.point: The chair's questions ask whether the citation can acknowledge long-acting analogue development without implying a fourth laureate, and whether B045 alone is enough.
responses.response: As a proposal for wording: the citation names the discovery of GLP-1 physiology and of its active form, and then says these discoveries made incretin-based therapies possible. The words 'made possible' credit the pathway to the drugs without naming the analogue developers as laureates. That reflects my view that excluding Knudsen is uncomfortable but defensible on discovery grounds, and the committee can say so in the prize motivation and the scientific background document. I would not accept wording that names an analogue or a drug. On the single-part question, I think B045 stands alone. Pairing it with B016 or B007 to add a second part would not remove the attribution problem, and it would risk diluting the weight of the choice. I would only revisit this if the attribution review showed that the Mojsov, Habener and Holst record cannot support a trio.

responses.point: A physiology-led trio of Holst, Drucker and Mojsov credits the people who established what the hormone is and does, and the exclusion of Knudsen is the weak point of a discovery-based reading.
responses.response: I agree with you on the principle, and I changed from my opening proposal, which put Knudsen in the trio, for the same reason. The person who designs a long-acting molecule has made an important contribution to medicine, but the Nobel will points to the discovery. I would add one condition to your position. Your trio is acceptable only if the priority record for the active peptide is checked against the primary papers, because nobody has audited it. If that check showed Habener's role to be larger than Mojsov's, the allocation of the third place would need to be reopened. I would raise that now so it is not discovered after the vote.

responses.point: Optogenetics is a transformative general-purpose method with early clinical use in vision restoration, ranked second, and the problem is credit among six people.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics changed neuroscience, and I do not dispute its importance. For this year I cannot support it as a preferred part. Six credited names exceed the cap, and any three would exclude Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck without a scientific reason that I could defend. The clinical benefit so far is small compared with incretin therapy. I would keep it as a candidate for a later year when the committee has decided how to treat a method of this kind, and I do not list it as an alternative now.

uncertainties: The relative priority of Mojsov, Habener and Holst for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide and its insulinotropic action is still unaudited, and Habener is outside the credited names.
Whether the committee reads the achievement as the physiology and active peptide, as I do, or as the drug class, which would move Knudsen into the trio.
Whether the 'made possible' wording is enough for members who find the exclusion of Knudsen unacceptable.
How CAR-T credit should be allocated among June, Sadelain, Rosenberg and Eshhar if the committee ever takes up B016.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I find no documented involvement with any credited name on the shortlist, and I do not request recusal. My research is in autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is not the subject of any shortlisted discovery. Working at the same institution as some colleagues or candidates does not establish a personal tie, and I have not inferred one.
